parts.title: Unraveling the Mammals of a Non-Protected Area in Tibet: How Many Kinds Live There, How They Interact, and Why They Need Protecting
parts.abstract:
Simple Summary

Human activities such as destroying natural habitats and overgrazing (letting too many farm animals feed on the land) are badly damaging ecosystems and causing large drops in the variety of mammals. Protected areas, such as national parks and nature reserves, play a vital role in keeping land mammals safe. But some places that are not protected, which we call non-protected areas, also help keep a rich variety of life and healthy, working ecosystems. It is essential to find out how valuable the mammal species in these important non-protected areas are for conservation.

In this study, we used camera traps, which are motion-triggered cameras that take pictures when an animal walks past, to survey Luolong County in Tibet, a non-protected area with great potential for protecting wildlife. We found that this area is a healthy, intact ecosystem. It has more species, and a greater variety of them, in scrub (low, bushy plant cover) and in evergreen forests. Important species live there, including plant-eaters such as musk deer, Chinese serow and woolly hares, and meat-eaters such as common leopards, snow leopards, red foxes and stone martens. The times when these species were detected are also linked to each other through features of the environment.

These results widen our understanding of how good the habitat is for rare species, and of the balance between endangered prey and their predators in Tibet's non-protected areas. They also show how important these areas are for conservation efforts.
parts.introduction_first:
We now live in what scientists call the Anthropocene, the age in which human activity is changing the planet. In this age, human activities are having a big effect on ecosystems, and this is reducing the vital services they provide, such as clean water and food [1]. Practices that cannot last, such as destroying habitats, bringing in invasive species (plants and animals that spread into places where they do not belong) and overusing natural resources, are causing widespread loss of biodiversity, the variety of living things. Rare wildlife is hit especially hard [2].

Protected areas, such as national parks and nature reserves, play a crucial role in conserving land mammals and biodiversity as a whole [3]. Mammal species generally support key jobs in ecosystems [4]. They are also often "umbrella species": protecting one of them also protects the many other species that share its home [5]. This is why it matters to understand how mammals are doing, especially as forests are being cut down faster and faster around the world [6]. Forests that have been damaged or disturbed tend to hold fewer kinds of mammals, which means the community of animals living there is less varied [7].

Recent research has also looked at how many species live in a place, how long they stay there, and how quickly new species move in, to understand patterns in diversity [8]. Researchers have also studied functional traits, such as what an animal eats and how big its body is. These traits act as signs of how healthy a community is and how it responds to changes in the environment [9,10]. They help show how animals adapt to their roles in ecosystems [11], and they help us judge how easily a community could be harmed and how well it could bounce back [12]. Studies also show that mammal communities in similar habitats tend to have similar sets of functional traits and respond in the same way to pressures from the environment, even when the actual species living there are different [13].
parts.conclusion:
6. Conclusions

We found that the non-protected area of Luolong County in Tibet is an intact ecosystem. It has more species, and a greater variety of them, in scrub and evergreen forests, and it is home to important plant-eaters such as musk deer, Chinese serow and woolly hares. Meat-eaters such as common leopards, snow leopards, foxes and martens were also often detected. Mammal species were found more often farther away from human activities.

We showed that different habitats and seasons affected both the variety of species and the ways species interact. Each species also prefers certain habitats: blue sheep on southern slopes when there is snow, musk deer in mixed forests, and red foxes avoiding alpine meadows. Among the large meat-eaters, the activity times of snow leopards were negatively linked with woolly hares, meaning that when one was more active, the other tended to be less active. Common leopards showed a positive link with hares and a negative link with brown bears. Among the medium-sized meat-eaters, such as red foxes, cameras detected them more often when Chinese serow were present.

We found that camera traps are a vital tool for finding out which species are present, whether or not there is snow, in mountain landscapes. They also help us untangle the complex relationships among mammal species and the challenges of protecting them in remote parts of Tibet, China.
parts.introduction_rest:
The Tibetan Plateau, often called the "Roof of the World", is vital because of its unique and delicate ecosystems [14,15]. It is home to many kinds of mammals, including many that are found nowhere else on Earth and many that are endangered [15]. Its varied landscape and extreme climate create many different habitats, and these support a rich variety of mammals [16]. Among them are well-known endangered and near-threatened species, such as the snow leopard (Panthera uncia) and the common leopard (Panthera pardus), which shows how important this region is for nature [17].

Mammals play vital roles in ecosystems. Top predators, the hunters at the very top of the food chain, keep the numbers of their prey in check, while plant-eaters shape the vegetation [18]. Their relationships are complex. For example, snow leopards hunt blue sheep, and wolves hunt marmots, and these relationships shape how the ecosystem is built and how its animals behave [19]. They affect not only how populations rise and fall, but also how species behave, where they live and how they evolve [20]. Top predators even affect how their prey feed and how the vegetation is spread across the land [21].

Species also compete for the same resources, such as food and space, and this competition affects how the community changes over time [22,23]. It pushes species to adapt to different ecological niches, meaning different ways of making a living, so that they overlap less and meet each other less often, both in place and in time [24]. Understanding these relationships is crucial if we want to predict how wildlife will respond to changes in the environment and to protect conservation efforts [25].

Protecting the variety of mammals on the Tibetan Plateau is becoming harder and harder, because human activities are destroying habitats. These activities include building roads and other infrastructure, overgrazing and mining [26,27]. As settlements and roads spread, they damage habitats and also make it easier for people to reach the land. This leads to more disturbance and more hunting and other use of wildlife [28]. Climate change adds to the threat by changing temperature, rainfall and snowfall, and the amount of snow cover. These changes affect where species can live and how much food and other resources they can find [18,29]. On top of this, farm animals that roam freely compete with wild animals for resources and can spread diseases. Conflicts between people and wildlife, especially when meat-eaters kill livestock, often lead people to kill the animals in revenge, which puts species in danger [27,30].

For these reasons, we carried out research in Luolong County, Tibet, using camera traps. Our aim was to find out where species live and how many of them there are, in an important ecosystem known for its rich variety of life, and to support future conservation work [31]. We had three main goals.

First, we expected that features of the environment would shape how species interact and which habitats they prefer in non-protected areas [32,33]. These features were how close a place is to water, the type of habitat, how steep the slope is, which direction the slope faces, the height above sea level, measures of how green and leafy the plants are (called vegetation indices), temperature and snow cover.

Second, we expected that places with many kinds of mammals and complex relationships between them may be more easily harmed by human disturbance. In such places, nearby settlements and roads may speed up the damage to habitats and put more pressure on the variety of life [22,34,35].

Finally, we set out to identify the main challenges to conservation that come from human activities and climate change. We also tried to develop recommendations based on science to improve conservation plans. These would help protect wildlife and their habitats better, while encouraging local communities to live alongside nature in a way that can last.
parts.results:
3. Results

3.1. How Varied the Mammal Communities Were in Different Habitats

Our camera traps recorded 10,202 photographic events in total, counting every mammal species. We found more species, and a greater variety of them, across 28 habitats, whether those habitats were similar to each other or different. Three species were especially common: alpine musk deer (990 individuals), Chinese serow (742) and woolly hares (830) (Figure 2A–D). Himalayan marmots, plateau pikas and white-lipped deer, on the other hand, were detected less often.

Among the meat-eaters, common leopards (1029), red foxes (1237) and stone martens (532) were detected more often, while snow leopards, red dogs, mountain weasels and yellow-billed weasels were detected less often (Supplementary Tables S2 and S3; Figure 2A,B).

We then compared habitats using a statistical test called a Mann–U test, which checks whether two groups differ more than chance alone would usually produce. Scrub and evergreen coniferous forests (forests of cone-bearing trees that keep their leaves all year) had a statistically significantly higher variety of mammals than mixed forests and alpine meadows (U = 333.0, p < 0.01). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. For p < 0.01, that means less than 1% of the time. The difference between the two lower-variety habitats, mixed forests and alpine meadows, was not significant (U = 204.0, p = 0.120) (Figure 3A,B). In other words, we could not show a difference between them.

The number of mammal species, and their variety, also changed significantly between snowy and snow-free days (U = 211, p < 0.05) (Figure S1).

We also looked at how far places were from human settlements, from water and from roads. The number of species rose with distance from human settlements (R2 = 0.711, p < 0.001; Figure 4B), from water (R2 = 0.441, p = 0.041; Figure 4C) and from roads (R2 = 0.881, p < 0.023; Figure 4D). R2 tells us how much of the variation in the number of species a pattern accounts for, from 0 (none) to 1 (all of it). The number of species was highest at moderate elevations (R2 = 0.721, p < 0.021; Figure 4G).

A rarefaction curve shows how many species turn up as more and more camera records are added. Ours showed a low overall variety, with around 25 mammal species identified (Figure 3A). We also used two common measures of variety, the Simpson and Shannon indices. Both take into account how many species there are and how evenly the animals are spread among them. Both were higher in scrub, coniferous forests and alpine meadows, but lower in mixed forests (Figure 3B). Figure S1C–F shows further significant differences in the number of species and in how many animals there were across habitats.

3.2. Which Places Mammals Chose: Predators and Prey

3.2.1. Prey Species

For each prey species, we looked for the model that best explained how often it was detected over time. We used linear mixed models (LMMs). These are statistical models that can test several factors at once while allowing for the fact that some cameras are simply busier than others. We call this allowance a random effect, here for each camera.

To choose the best model, we used a score called AICc. It rewards a model for matching the data well but penalizes it for being more complicated than it needs to be. A lower score is better. K is the number of factors in the model.

For blue sheep, the best model linked detection strongly to the direction a slope faced, especially southern slopes when there was snow. The camera random effect was 0.024 (Table 1 and Table 2).

For Chinese serow, the best model included NDVI and scrub habitats (K = 4). NDVI is a measure of how green and leafy the plants are. This model pointed to a preference for scrub, although greener plants (higher NDVI) actually went along with fewer serow (Table 1 and Table 2).

For musk deer, the best model included snow and habitat type (K = 8). Snowy days meant fewer detections, which suggests that musk deer avoid snow cover, and they preferred mixed forests.

For white-lipped deer, the best model used two factors (K = 7; AICc = 163.39). These deer kept away from roads and liked scrub.

For woolly hares, three factors mattered (K = 8; AICc = 4340.50). Alpine meadows increased detections, while rain and snow, evergreen forests and distance from water decreased sightings.

For plateau pikas, two factors gave the best prediction (K = 7; AICc = 2573.09), and these pikas favored alpine meadows and scrub.

For rhesus macaque, moderate elevation and greener plants (higher NDVI) mattered most (K = 4; AICc = 249.70).

Finally, for Himalayan marmots, two factors gave the best model (K = 4; AICc = 412.76). Lower elevations reduced detections, while the other factors were not significant.

3.2.2. Predators

For brown bears, four factors mainly shaped how often they were detected over time: temperature, snow cover, slope and habitat type (K = 10; AICc = 487.11). Warmer temperatures and the presence of snow reduced detections, while bears preferred mixed forests.

Grey wolves kept away from roads and human settlements (K = 5; AICc = 283.62). Badgers were best explained by three factors, and they were detected less often when it was warmer and when there was snow (K = 6; AICc = 136.52).

For leopard cats, one factor, slope, explained detection, and these cats tended to avoid steep areas (K = 4; AICc = 191.33). Eurasian lynx were driven by two factors: they avoided northern slopes and favored shrub zones (K = 7; AICc = 110.57).

Common leopards were affected by three factors. They were detected more often when there was snow, but they kept away from roads (K = 6; AICc = 385.22). Snow leopards depended on four factors. They favored mixed and coniferous forests, with no clear link to temperature or altitude (K = 10; AICc = 1693.88).

Red foxes preferred scrub and avoided alpine meadows (K = 6; AICc = 1193.30). Red dogs were best explained by two factors, mainly keeping away from roads (K = 7; AICc = 82.53). Yellow-billed weasels were affected by four factors and tended to avoid rain while favoring coniferous forests (K = 9; AICc = 47.08). Stone martens were mainly affected by the presence of water, which they avoided (K = 3; AICc = 404.70).

3.3. How the Animals Interacted: Predators and Prey

3.3.1. Meat-Eaters

To study how the activity times of two species were linked, we used a model that tests whether the activity of one species rises or falls along with the activity of another. The intercept is the number the model gives for that link. A positive intercept means the two tend to be active at the same times. A negative one means that when one is more active, the other tends to be less active. The standard error (SE) shows how uncertain each estimate is.

The activity times of snow leopards were mainly negatively linked with those of woolly hares. The overall model was significant (F(1, 261) = 5.715, p < 0.017), but it explained only a small part of the variation (R2 = 0.017).

Common leopards showed significant links with both brown bears and woolly hares. Their baseline activity was 0.624 (SE = 0.035, p < 0.001). Woolly hares had a positive link with them (intercept = 0.109, SE = 0.044, p < 0.013; Figure S2), while brown bears had a negative link (intercept = −0.143, SE = 0.050, p < 0.004; Figure S2). The combined model was significant (F(2, 260) = 6.138, p < 0.002), with an adjusted R2 of 0.037.

Red fox activity was positively related to Chinese serow, with intercepts of 0.407 (SE = 0.046, p < 0.001; Figure S2) and 0.194 (SE = 0.086, p < 0.025). The overall model was significant (F(1, 261) = 5.017, p < 0.025) and explained a small part of the variation (R2 = 0.015).

Leopard cat activity times were negatively linked with yellow-billed weasels (Figure S2h). The intercept was 0.659 (SE = 0.037, p < 0.001), and the effect of yellow-billed weasels was close to significant (intercept = −0.112, SE = 0.058, p < 0.056). The model was only just significant (F(1, 261) = 3.684, p < 0.056), with a slight negative link (adjusted R2 = 0.010).

Eurasian lynx activity was negatively linked with woolly hares (intercept = 0.405, SE = 0.051, p < 0.001; Figure S2p) and positively linked with white-lipped deer (intercept = 0.278, SE = 0.077, p < 0.003; Figure S2o). This model explained about 5.8% of the variation (F(1, 260) = 9.191, p < 0.013; R2 = 0.058).

In a similar way, grey wolf activity was positively linked with white-lipped deer (intercept = 0.363, SE = 0.043, p < 0.001; Figure S2z), which accounted for roughly 1.6% of the variation (F(1, 261) = 5.456, p < 0.020). Red fox activity was positively linked with musk deer (intercept = 0.488, SE = 0.017, p < 0.001; Figure S2r), explaining about 1.9% of the variation (F(1, 261) = 6.129, p < 0.013).

Stone marten activity was positively linked with hares (intercept = 3.286, SE = 2.703, p < 0.001; Figure S2f), which contributed around 10.1% to the model (F(1, 261) = 5.092, p < 0.003). Lastly, yellow-billed weasel activity was negatively linked with leopard cats (intercept = 0.589, SE = 0.045, p < 0.001), and the model explained 1.1% of the variation (F(1, 261) = 3.684, p < 0.056; Figure S2u).

3.3.2. How Plant-Eaters and Omnivores Interacted in Time

The activity times of Himalayan marmots were negatively linked with those of brown bears (Figure S2d). Marmots showed significant positive links with stone martens and Tibetan pikas (intercept = 3.130, SE = 4.749, p < 0.001; Tibetan pika intercept = 1.399, SE = 6.189, p < 0.024; Figure S2s). The brown bear intercept was −1.089 (SE = 4.736, p < 0.022), and the stone marten intercept was 1.000 (SE = 4.129, p < 0.001).

Tibetan pikas showed a significant positive link in activity with Himalayan marmots (intercept = 0.478, SE = 0.024, p < 0.001; marmot intercept = 0.089, SE = 0.040, p < 0.028; Figure S2a).

Woolly hare activity was negatively linked with snow leopards. Eurasian lynx activity was positively linked with snow leopards and brown bears. The woolly hare intercept was 0.455 (SE = 0.089, p < 0.001). The snow leopard intercept was 0.201 (SE = 0.084, p < 0.017; Figure S2l). The snow leopard intercept was also −0.142 (SE = 0.070, p < 0.044; Figure S2x). The eurasian lynx intercept was −0.151 (SE = 0.072, p = 0.036; Figure S2n), and the brown bear intercept was 0.201 (SE = 0.068, p < 0.003; Figure S2k).

Brown bear activity was negatively linked with snow leopards and Himalayan marmots, but positively linked with woolly hare activity. The brown bear intercept was 0.622 (SE = 0.061, p < 0.001). The snow leopard intercept was −0.214 (SE = 0.074, p < 0.004; Figure S2b). The woolly hare intercept was 0.156 (SE = 0.053, p < 0.003; Figure S2e), and the Himalayan marmot intercept was −0.098 (SE = 0.052; p < 0.059; Figure S2c).

Musk deer activity showed a significant positive link with red dogs (intercept = 0.262, SE = 0.053, p < 0.001), and the red dog intercept was 0.243 (SE = 0.098, p < 0.013; Figure S2q). In the same way, Chinese serow activity was positively linked with red foxes (intercept = 0.418, SE = 0.027, p < 0.001; Figure S2w; red fox intercept = 0.096, SE = 0.043, p < 0.025), and the model was significant (F(1, 261) = 5.017, p < 0.025).

White-lipped deer activity was negatively linked with Himalayan marmots. It showed significant positive links with Eurasian lynx and grey wolves. The white-lipped deer intercept was 0.462 (SE = 0.036, p < 0.001). The Eurasian lynx intercept was 0.142 (SE = 0.046, p < 0.002; Figure S2v), and the grey wolf intercept was 0.106 (SE = 0.048, p < 0.029; Figure S2y). The Himalayan marmot link was negative (−0.108, SE = 0.037, p < 0.007; Figure S2t).
parts.discussion:
4. Discussion

We recorded 25 mammal species across 28 habitats in Luolong County, in southeastern Tibet. Some of these habitats were similar to each other and some were different. We found that the ecosystem was well balanced, with top predators (the biggest hunters, such as snow leopards and wolves), medium-sized meat-eaters and prey animals all present across the different habitats. However, the mammal species tended to stay away from the nearest villages and roads. These findings confirm that human activities and the building of roads and other structures affect both how many kinds of animals there are and where they live, in many different ways. They also suggest that protected areas should be declared here, to act as vital shelters that keep the variety of life safe [53]. Still, we know little about the variety of life in high mountain regions. With this in mind, our data suggest that this area should be considered as a protected area in the future.

4.1. How the Mix of Species Differs Between Habitats

Checking the variety of life in a place is a crucial way to record whether rare and endangered species are still there and how they are doing [31]. When there are few species, there is often less backup. Different species often do similar jobs in an ecosystem, so if one disappears, another can often take over. When there are few species, losing a key one can therefore do far more harm to the ecosystem and to the vital services it provides than losing one species in a richer place. Setting a starting record of the variety of life, and then checking wildlife numbers again and again over time, are essential steps for judging whether protected areas and efforts to bring animals back to old homes are working [54]. Red dogs and Tibetan foxes were detected extremely rarely during our camera-trap survey. Even so, our findings suggest that most mammal species prefer habitats such as coniferous forests (forests of cone-bearing trees like pines), broad-leaved forests of trees that drop their leaves in winter, and scrub.

The variety of species also went down as certain human and geographical features increased. Areas closer to rivers, roads and villages tended to hold fewer kinds of animals. In addition, most species in our study area live at middle to high elevations. Other studies that looked at the variety of life across seasons or across different places and times, including top predators, medium-sized meat-eaters and medium to large prey animals, also found that habitat quality changes from one of these areas to another [47].

We also found that most mammals tend to live in places with little human activity and farther from roads. Other studies of how mammals use space have seen the same pattern [55]. Our camera-trap survey successfully identified nine mammal species that are classed as rare. This shows how useful the method is for collecting information on shy animals that are hard to spot, and how it can improve our picture of the variety of life in the region. Further surveys over larger areas or longer periods could help confirm the activity patterns we saw. They could also deepen our understanding of what rare species need to survive, and support better conservation planning for Tibet's mammals, based on solid evidence, as recent studies in China have pointed out [56]. Those studies also show that climate factors, such as snow cover and low temperatures, and grazing pressure strongly affect where species live. For example, woolly hares tend to avoid snowy areas, while snow prefers steep slopes with low NDVI, a measure of how green and leafy the plants are.

4.2. How Often Species Were Detected, and How This Is Linked to Their Habitat

4.2.1. Plant-Eaters and Animals That Eat Both Plants and Animals

We found that blue sheep are more likely to be found on south-facing slopes on days when there is snow, but this pattern does not hold on days without snow. This seasonal change suggests that the direction a slope faces is a crucial factor in where blue sheep choose to live, as has been seen in Tibetan antelopes (Pantholops hodgsonii) [57]. The Chinese serow clearly prefers scrub, which probably gives it easy access to food. In winter, Chinese serow may feed on the twigs of plants in these scrub areas to meet its food needs, as has been seen in mainland serow (Capricornis sumatraensis) in Tangjiahe Natural Reserve in China [58]. Musk deer, on the other hand, favour mixed forests. They tend to avoid moving around much when it is snowy, since they were detected less often when snow was present [59].

White-lipped deer move around in clear ways that depend on human structures. They tend to avoid busy roads such as major highways, but they sometimes use smaller paths in forests, such as footpaths and routes used by farm animals, to get around. This differs from earlier results in China [60].

Woolly hares mainly live in alpine meadows, the high, open grasslands above the tree line, where they feed and do most of their other activities. We sometimes saw groups of two or three hares, but most of the time we detected them alone. Notably, woolly hares tend to avoid areas with more rain, evergreen mixed forests and places close to water. This consistency points to shared ways of adapting among hare (Lepus capensis) species, which help them find food efficiently and avoid predators in high mountain places [52]. The plateau pika (Ochotona curzoniae) was detected most often in alpine meadows and scrub, which shows that these habitats are key places for it. Pikas were sometimes seen in small groups of 1–2, but mostly alone. Notably, on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau this species is active during the day [61].

Rhesus macaques were detected more often in areas at middle elevations with higher NDVI, meaning greener, leafier plant cover. This suggests that places at middle heights with plenty of plants are vital for their survival. Such places probably offer important food, such as fruits and plants, as well as good shelter from the local challenges of the environment [62].

We noticed that marmots tend to be detected at the highest elevations, and that they favour gentle slopes, open meadows and grasslands. In addition, some marmots at the edges of scrub areas are mainly active during the day, as has been seen in Nepal [63]. These habitat preferences and activity patterns confirm that gentle, grassy areas are vital for marmots to find food and survive [64]. Brown bears were detected less often in cold, snowy weather, which suggests they tend to avoid harsh winter conditions. They prefer mixed forests, and they choose these mainly because of the shape of the land and the height, rather than because of how close they are to human activities such as roads or villages (Frąckowiak et al., 2014) [65].

4.2.2. Large Meat-Eaters and Medium-Sized Meat-Eaters

Gray wolves generally avoid busy roads and areas near places where farm animals graze. This is probably a way to reduce conflict with people, since being close to villages, roads and grazing areas raises the chance of running into people. Interestingly, we did see some exceptions: we occasionally detected wolf packs near trails and tracks used by farm animals. Most sightings involved groups of 2 to 3 wolves, and sometimes packs of up to five. Gray wolves often prefer areas with lots of farm animals, and they may hunt or come into conflict with people near villages [66] and near pens for farm animals [51].

The leopard cat tends to avoid steep slopes and prefers to move along smaller paths. In contrast, research shows that leopard cats usually rest in natural places where it is hard to see, such as areas with shrubs, reeds and stones, and these places are also far from areas with a lot of human activity [67]. The red fox tends to prefer scrub and avoids alpine meadows, roads and evergreen forests, since roads have a clearly negative effect on where it chooses to live [68], and it prefers land with herbs or shrubs in China [58]. The yellow-billed weasel seems to be held back by rain and snow, and it prefers evergreen forests, probably staying away from rainy seasons so that it is less active in bad conditions. It tends to stay away from rivers and lakes, perhaps because of the risk of flooding or other dangers. Similar studies suggest that medium-sized meat-eaters often keep conflicts with top predators and with people to a minimum, across both space and time [69]. Eurasian lynx also favour scrub, which gives them important shelter for hiding from predators and for hunting small to medium prey such as hares and rodents. This choice of habitat shows how important scrub is for keeping lynx populations healthy in our study area [70]. Snow cover does not significantly change how often snow leopards are detected. This toughness probably comes from their special adaptations, such as thick fur and large paws suited to snowy ground, and from their flexible ways of finding food [34]. Snow leopards tend to avoid roads, which shows the harm that long, straight structures such as roads do to their habitat [71].

Common leopards mainly favour mixed forests and evergreen coniferous forests, which fits with their nature: they can adapt to many things, but they still depend on forests. These forests have many layers. A thick canopy of treetops gives them places to hide, the lower layers of plants give them places to hunt prey such as deer and wild boar, and tree hollows are ideal for resting or raising cubs [71]. Compared with open ground, these forests also have steadier local weather, which lets common leopards stay active and breed all year round [72]. Red dogs (dholes) tend to avoid roads and evergreen coniferous forests. They probably avoid roads because they are sensitive to disturbance by people: roads bring them into contact with vehicles, farm animals and villages, and this can upset the teamwork they need to hunt together in undisturbed places [73]. In the same way, they may avoid evergreen coniferous forests because there is less prey there, since these forests usually hold fewer plant-eaters, and because the thick plants can get in the way of chasing prey [9].

4.3. How the Species Interact With Each Other

The activity times of snow leopards were linked only to the detection of hares, and the link was negative. This suggests that hares are not a main part of their diet, and that snow leopards probably depend more on other prey [74]. Having more of other prey, such as blue sheep, in the study area may affect how snow leopards behave [24].

The activity times of common leopards were positively linked with the presence of hares, which shows that hares are probably an important prey animal for them. Common leopard activity was also negatively linked with brown bears [18]. This probably reflects a way of avoiding direct conflict [75], and it reduces conflict between species that share the same habitat [76].

Red foxes and Chinese serow tend to be active at the same times. This shows that they probably live side by side without much competition or avoiding each other in shared habitats. According to optimal foraging theory, the idea that animals try to get the most food for the least effort, both predators and prey use strategies that help them survive and have young, by balancing the energy they spend against the chances to find food [77]. The activity times of leopard cats tend to be the opposite of those of yellow-billed weasels, probably as a way to reduce conflict between the two. This suggests that these predators either avoid meeting each other directly or change their behaviour to compete less [78] and change what they eat [79].

Eurasian lynx activity was positively linked with the presence of both hares and white-lipped deer. This suggests that lynx may be active at the same times as their prey, and that eurasian lynx sometimes hunt both small and large prey [80]. Red fox activity seems to be linked with the movements of musk deer, while stone marten activity lines up with the presence of marmots [81]. In addition, yellow-billed weasel activity was negatively linked with leopard cat activity, which points to possible ways of avoiding each other to reduce conflict [48]. Among the small meat-eaters, the stone marten and the leopard cat are similar in size and diet, so they may compete when they live together, especially since both like to chase small prey [82].

Himalayan marmot activity tends to drop when brown bears are around, probably as a way of avoiding being eaten, since bears may hunt them [83]. In contrast, marmots are more active near stone martens and plateau pikas, which suggests little competition and that they may be able to live alongside these species [84]. Hares, on the other hand, become less active when brown bears, common leopards and eurasian lynx are nearby, probably to avoid being eaten by these large predators [85]. Woolly hares, however, become more active around common leopards and bears. This may be because they share the same habitat preferences rather than because of a direct threat, or perhaps these predators focus on other prey, which makes hares relatively safe [18]. Musk deer become more active at the same time as red foxes, which shows that they neither avoid these predators nor usually escape them, suggesting little threat or conflict [86]. In the same way, Chinese serow also tend to be active when red foxes are present, which suggests they do not avoid this predator and may put up with it, unlike how they respond to other meat-eaters [79]. White-lipped deer, by contrast, are less active when Himalayan marmots are nearby, but more active when eurasian lynx and gray wolves are around. This pattern shows that prey animals actively change their behaviour, either seeking out or avoiding certain predators, to lower their risks and improve their chances of survival [19,76].

2. Materials and Methods: How We Did the Study

2.1. Where We Worked

We carried out this study in the southwestern part of Qamdo, in Luolong County (95°10′–95°50′ E, 30°10′–31°50′ N), in southeastern Tibet. The area lies along the upper part of the Nujiang River. It borders the northern part of the Hengduan Mountains, and its western edge meets the southeastern tip of the Nyainqêntanglha Mountains. The land is high, with an average height of about 3700 m above sea level, and it covers close to 8108 km². Most people here earn their living from farming crops and raising animals. They grow wheat, highland barley and rapeseed, and they raise yaks, goats and pigs [17]. People mostly live in villages and along roads. These are also the places where animals graze and where people harvest medicinal fungi such as caterpillar fungus (Ophiocordyceps sinensis) [17].

The climate is a temperate semi-arid monsoon climate, which means it is fairly dry and has a rainy season. This is typical of the southeastern Tibetan Plateau. The area gets plenty of sunshine, and temperatures change a lot through the year, with dry winters and mild summers. The average temperature over the year is about 5.5 °C. The hottest temperature ever recorded was 30.6 °C, and the coldest was −22.1 °C. About 424.6 mm of rain and snow falls each year, mostly between May and September. The region gets more than 2500 hours of sunshine a year, and it has about 120 days without frost.

Luolong County is home to an exceptionally wide variety of life, including about 25 species of mammals, both large and small [36]. Some of these species are important around the world. They include the white-lipped deer (Cervus albirostris), common leopard (Panthera pardus), leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis), red dog, also called the dhole (Cuon alpinus), red fox (Vulpes vulpes), pika (Ochotona curzoniae), Asian badger (Meles leucurus), yellow-throated marten (Martes flavigula), Himalayan weasel (Mustela sibirica), woolly hare (Lepus oiostolus), gray wolf (Canis lupus), alpine musk deer (Moschus chrysogaster), rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta), Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx), stone marten (Martes foina), mountain weasel (Mustela altaica), Himalayan marmot (Marmota himalayana), snow leopard (Panthera uncia), blue sheep (Pseudois nayaur), wild boar (Sus scrofa), Tibetan fox (Vulpes ferrilata), hog badger (Arctonyx collaris), Chinese serow (Capricornis milneedwardsii), yellow-billed weasel (Mustela sibirica) and brown bear (Ursus arctos). Having so many kinds of animals shows how rich and varied the region's wildlife is.

The plants here include conifer forests (forests of cone-bearing trees), shrublands and meadows. The conifer forests are mostly made up of Lijiang spruce (Picea likiangensis) and Engelmann fir (Abies georgei). The shrublands are mainly made up of plants such as Caragana, Berberis, Rhododendron and Spiraea. The meadows are mostly covered by sedges (Carex), which are grass-like plants. Figure 1 shows the landscape, and Table S1 lists the mammal species and how they are doing in China.

2.2. How We Collected the Data

2.2.1. Where We Set Up the Camera Traps

We used camera traps to find out how often each mammal species was detected over time, and which species were detected together [37,38]. First, we divided the study area into a grid of squares, each 5 km by 5 km, and placed camera traps carefully within each square. We also adjusted the placement to suit the conditions on the ground. Squares with overgrazing had fewer cameras. Some squares had 2–4 extra cameras, because more mammal species were found there and people disturbed them less. This made our survey partly systematic, and it helped us detect animals more often [39,40]. We did not use any bait or scent to draw animals to the cameras.

Each camera ran for about six months (180 days) and worked steadily for 4 to 5 months. Every camera stayed fixed in one place and never moved. The cameras ran without a break, so there was no gap between one picture and the next.

Sometimes a camera takes several pictures or video clips of the same animal, or of the same group of animals of the same species, one after another. We call these repeated records, or duplicates. We counted them as duplicates when they met all of the following conditions: (1) they were taken by the same camera at the same fixed spot; (2) we could tell from the pictures that they showed the same species; and (3) they were taken within a set time window, so that they were probably just the same animal or group staying in the camera's view. In other words, they did not show a separate, independent visit.

We collected data from November 2019 to June 2023 at 159 camera sites. We grouped these sites into 28 locations, each covering about 1000 km², based on whether their landscapes were similar or different. The locations ranged in height from 1878 to 3138 m above sea level. Each location had two or four cameras at different spots within the same grid square. Some cameras faced each other, so they could record the same scene from two sides. We usually fixed the cameras to rocks or tree trunks about 50 cm above the ground. Each photo was labelled with extra information: the date, the time, the moon phase, the temperature and the type of habitat [41]. We used two models of camera trap, the Bolym BG962-X36W and the SG2060-K (made by Bolymedia Communications, Shenzhen, China). During the day they record colour pictures and video, and at night they record black-and-white pictures and video. They react to movement in 0.20 seconds.

2.2.2. Recording Which Mammals Live in Each Place

We loaded all the raw pictures and videos from the cameras into a computer program called Camerabase 2.0. We then removed the useless records by hand. These included blank pictures and false triggers, which happen when plants, light or a camera fault sets off the camera. For each useful record, we noted the camera site, the exact time, the species and whether it was a new, independent visit.

To decide what counted as a new visit, we used a time window that depended on the species. For animals that live alone or move around a lot, the window was 30 minutes. For animals that live in groups or stay in one place, it was 15 minutes. The camera's software sorted the records by site and species and put them in time order. It then automatically marked any record that came within the time window after the first one as a duplicate. Three researchers checked these possible duplicates by hand, and a senior researcher fixed any disagreements, taking into account unusual animal behaviour. We confirmed that the duplicates were truly repeated records, and we kept only the first record of each independent visit. Finally, we randomly checked 10% of the records to make sure the filtering had no mistakes. This kept our data consistent for the ecological analysis.

For each mammal species, we recorded every independent visit, and noted whether there was snow or not. We left out of the final analysis any videos that showed people, farm animals or things we could not identify [22]. We counted the number of independent visits for each species, following the methods described in [42,43]. This let us measure how many species there were and how that number built up as we added more cameras. To measure how much survey effort we had put in, we multiplied the total number of cameras by the number of days they ran. We counted each species' detection rate over a 24-hour period as a separate event. When a group of animals appeared, such as wolves or blue sheep, we counted each animal in the group separately [44]. We sorted the habitats into several types: alpine meadows or grasslands, evergreen conifer forests, mixed forests (with both broad-leaved and needle-leaved trees), and scrub or shrubland. We used worldwide maps of plant cover from a website (https://data.tpdc.ac.cn) to do this [39].

We also measured how far each camera was from water (such as rivers and streams), from the nearest road, and from the nearest human settlement or grazing area, all in metres. We took these distances from a mapping website (www.webmap.cn) [45]. We worked out the shape of the land, including how steep the slope was, which direction it faced, and the height above sea level (in metres). For this we used digital elevation models, which are computer maps of land height, from a free online source (https://www.gscloud.cn) [46]. We also downloaded the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) of the study area from the same website (https://data.tpdc.ac.cn) [18]. This is a measure, based on satellite images, of how green and leafy the plants are. The temperature data came from the camera traps, and the average yearly rainfall came from another website (https://www.worldclim.org). We measured and combined all of these environmental factors using a mapping program called ArcGIS 10.2.

2.2.3. How Mammals Interact, and How This Links to Their Habitat

We worked out how often each species was detected over time, including pairs of predators and their prey. We put the data into separate Excel sheets for meat-eaters and for plant-eaters [47]. We then sorted the data by camera site, and also by whether there was snow or not. We also recorded the habitat features linked to each species. Species that were detected very rarely (fewer than 30 times) were left out of the final analysis of habitat preferences, such as the wild boar.

We also studied the 24-hour activity pattern of each species, using the times on the camera records, which were set to Tibetan local time [48]. We worked out each species' activity times from the times on its videos, which were labelled with both the date and the camera's ID. We sorted the activity times into three groups [19]. Nocturnal animals are active mainly from one hour after sunset until one hour before sunrise. Diurnal animals are active mainly from one hour after sunrise until one hour before sunset. Crepuscular animals are active around dawn and dusk, from one hour before sunrise to one hour after sunrise, and from one hour before sunset to one hour after sunset. We combined these into one set of data, called activity times.

2.3. How We Analysed the Data

2.3.1. How Many Species There Are, and How the Count Grows

First, we wanted to know whether we had enough camera sites to find most of the species living there. To check, we pooled the data from all the cameras. We then looked at how many species we found, and how that number built up, as we added cameras at different sites. We estimated the number of species we had actually seen by looking at how often rare species turned up, following the method in [49].

To measure the variety of species, we used a set of measures called Hill numbers, calculated with a software package for the R programming language called iNEXT (version 3.0.2). Each Hill number is set by a value called q. When q = 0, it simply counts the number of species. When q = 1, it is called Shannon diversity, and when q = 2, it is called Simpson diversity. As q gets bigger, rare species count for less in the result [49]. We also drew rarefaction curves for each camera placement feature. These curves show how the number of species found grows as more cameras are added.

We measured the variety of species in four ways: the number of species, how many animals there were, the diversity measures, and the feeding groups (trophic guilds) [44]. We did this for four habitat types, split by whether there was snow or not. The number of species was simply the total number of species the cameras detected. We calculated the variety of species from the camera traps using this formula [50]:

D = (∑S_i = 1, pi2)

Here, S is the number of species at each site, and pi is the share of all the detections at that site that belonged to each species.

We used the Shannon and Simpson measures to judge the variety of species. These measures take into account both how many species there are and how evenly the animals are spread among them. We also used accumulation curves [49]. We drew rarefaction curves for the species to compare the number of species and the detection rates between sites [44,49].

To show how certain our estimates were, we calculated 95% confidence intervals, which are ranges that show how much an estimate could vary. We used a method called the unconditional variance method, which shuffles the data 1000 times to see how much the results change, following [42]. We also compared the number of species between habitat types and between places with and without snow. For this we used Mann–Whitney U-tests, which check whether the values in one group tend to be higher than in another without assuming the data follow a bell-shaped curve. Because we made several comparisons, we adjusted the p-values to allow for this, and we judged statistical significance from the adjusted values [37]. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone.

We ran all the analyses in R (version 4.4.1). We used iNEXT (version 3.0.2) for the diversity and rarefaction analyses. We used dplyr (version 1.1.4), tidyr (version 1.3.1), ggplot2 (version 3.5.1), tibble (version 3.2.1) and patchwork (version 1.3.0) to organise the data and draw the graphs.

2.3.2. Feeding Groups and Their Links to Habitat

We wanted to find out how each mammal species was linked to the habitat features. To do this, we built 16 linear mixed-effects models, using the R packages lme4 (version 1.1-35.5) and ggplot2 (version 3.5.1). A linear mixed-effects model is a statistical tool that looks for straight-line relationships between a result and several possible causes at the same time. It can also allow for the fact that some measurements are grouped together, here by camera. We included the camera's ID as a random effect, which means the model allowed for the fact that cameras at the same site may give similar results.

Before building the models, we checked how closely the habitat features were linked to each other. We left out any features that were too closely linked to another, with a correlation above 0.7, so that the models would not be confused by features that carry almost the same information. We calculated the size of each effect using the R package mvnormalTest (version 1.0.1).

In each model, the result we were trying to explain was how often a particular species was detected over time. The habitat features were the possible causes, called fixed effects. To choose the best model, we used a score called the corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc), which rewards a model for fitting the data well but penalises it for being too complicated. We also used the difference in this score between models (delta AICc) and the model weights, which show how much support each model has compared with the others. We did this with the R package AICcmodavg (version 2.3-3) [51]. To judge whether each habitat feature mattered, we looked at its estimated effect, its standard error (a measure of how uncertain that estimate is) and its 95% confidence interval.

2.3.3. How Meat-Eaters, Plant-Eaters and Omnivores Interact

We studied how species interact using linear regression models, which look for straight-line relationships between one measurement and others. For each target species, we used its activity times over a 24-hour period as the result to be explained. We used the activity times of other species as the possible causes. We also checked for habitat features that were too closely linked to each other. We found that the activity times of macaques caused problems in the models for farm animals and people, so we left macaques out of those models [52].

We chose the best model using three measures. The first was the degrees of freedom, which reflect how much independent information the model has. The second was the adjusted R-squared, which shows how much of the variation in the result the model explains, adjusted for how many causes it includes. The third was the F-statistic, which tests whether the model as a whole explains the result better than chance would. We set the cut-off for statistical significance at p < 0.05. This means we called a result statistically significant when, if there were really no link, a pattern this strong would appear by chance less than 5% of the time. We ran all of these analyses in RStudio version 4.0.5.
